Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:75: To understand the matter further, we say that the sustenances mentioned there in the statements are four: first, the sustenance of the general people from heaven and earth — the meaning being that their sustenance is prepared for them and they eat their sufficiency whenever they need. Second, the sustenance of the poor, from the attribute of righteousness [tzedek]. Third, the sustenance of the sick, from the attribute called "heaven," as it is said (Psalms 41:4), "the LORD will sustain him upon the bed of illness." Fourth, the sustenance of the Torah scholar, from the side of Chochmah — each according to the preparation of the purification of his body and soul, so will the supernal spirituality be drawn and rest upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:76: Now, the poor — their sustenance is from the attribute of righteousness, because they are broken and lowly, their heart broken and crushed; so their sustenance is finer, since their sustenance is not readily available and prepared for them whenever they wish. Therefore a flow is drawn to them from the attribute of righteousness, that their sustenance be blessed and they have existence until the time their food arrives.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:77: And the sick, who do not eat bread at all but only some drink, and sometimes do not even drink any drink, and their sustenance is the shrinking of the fat and blood within them — their sustenance is more spiritual, since the bodily powers have already ceased functioning, and from the side of the supernal attribute mentioned, existence is drawn for their soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:78: And Torah scholars occupied with Torah — their sustenance is entirely sustenance for the soul. That is, the Shechinah bestows their sustenance from Chochmah, as it says (Proverbs 31:14), "she brings her bread from afar." And it is already known that the word "far" [rachok] and "distances" [merchakim] are all a Name. And this bread is physical — bread of their sustenance, through which their body is provided for — but within that bread there is a supernal spirituality, such that a single meal of it suffices to give existence to the body for three days and the like, and it contains spirituality for the enlightenment of Torah and its secrets. Proof of this is what they said in the Zohar (portion Lech Lecha, 94b) regarding the village of Tarsha, where they said to Rabbi Abba that that place had earned merit for them regarding Torah, and he said: this is our custom — every night we sleep half the night and occupy ourselves with Torah the other half, and when we arise in the morning, the scents of the field and the flowing rivers illuminate the Torah for us and settle it in our hearts. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose. Behold, it is explicit that the scents of the field illuminated for them the secrets of Torah. The reason is that through the occupation with Torah in which they engaged in that place, the Holy One, blessed be He, would draw down a spiritual flow into those plants, and through this they gained wisdom. In this same manner, into the food of Torah scholars — into that bread or other sustenance — a flow of soul-sustenance is drawn for the enlightenment of Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:79: This is what is explained in Tikkunim (45b), which we copied in the Gate of Love (ch. 6), that the Shechinah has, for some, the bringing down of bodily sustenance, and for others, the bringing down of the sustenance of the neshamah, which is the sustenance of Torah. One should not interpret this to mean that it is Torah-sustenance alone, for if he ate nothing at all he would die; rather the intent is that the greater part of his sustenance is sustenance for the neshamah, and even though he does eat physically, since it is fine, the neshamah is the one being nourished and it dominates in the enlightenment of Torah, while the body is weak.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:80: Support for this matter we find in the Zohar (portion Vayera, 104a), these are his words: they said there that the angels who visited Abraham our father, peace be upon him, all that they ate was consumed through a fire-offering, and even though the verse says they ate, the intent is that they were nourished by the kindness [chesed] of Abraham. And he said: therefore it is written "and they ate" — they caused themselves to be nourished from the side of Abraham, and therefore nothing remained of what Abraham gave them. In similar fashion, a person needs to drink from that cup of blessing in order to merit that blessing from above; those [angels] also ate from what Abraham prepared for them in order to merit being nourished from the side of Abraham, since from that side sustenance issues to all the supernal angels. Thus far his words. Behold, it is explicit that although nothing remained at all of the physical food they ate, since it was consumed by a fire-offering, nevertheless they were spiritually nourished from the side of the kindness they ate through Abraham. So it is with the sustenance of Torah scholars: although the food in their bodies is digested, spiritual sustenance remains for their soul, since their sustenance is drawn from Chochmah, which is above Chesed, and they can stand without eating for three or four days; and while they are occupied with Torah they are nourished spiritually by that very Torah they engage in. If so, without doubt this matter is found only among those whose Torah is their profession.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:81: In this manner it is resolved how Rashbi, peace be upon him, and his son sat in a cave for thirteen years and were nourished by eating carobs (Shabbat 33b), because the supernal attribute of Chochmah was their sustenance, and it is finer and more spiritual than all the other lower attributes, and does not dwell in the body because of its fineness, but gives spiritual sustenance to Ruach and Neshamah, which belong to Torah scholars — for the ordinary Torah scholar holds the middle line and has Ruach and Neshamah, and therefore his sustenance from above is fine and spiritual. And likewise we find they said in Tikkunim that Chochmah is the irrigation of the tree, and it is the soul of life (Tikkunei Zohar 96a) that spreads within the attributes to give them life, and does not dwell in the attributes except as the spreading of Da'at and Binah within them, as my teacher, peace be upon him, explained in the Idra. Therefore Torah scholars who hold onto Torah hold onto the principal thing and the root, for Torah is more internal than all the commandments, as will be explained in its place, and their sustenance is Chochmah, which does not dwell except in their Ruach and Neshamah, not in the body, even though it does eat; therefore the soul dominates and the body is weak.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:82: And because Torah scholars' main sustenance is for the soul, as explained, they can therefore stand two or three days without eating at all, since Torah-sustenance is their sustenance, and it is what gives them existence. And if this matter is found in penitents [ba'alei teshuvah], we may say that the power of repentance nourishes them, as is written in Tikkunim (113b) that penitents have an additional soul, and this additional soul, which is by the power of repentance, can nourish them so they stand three days without eating; and also the trait of the righteous, to be content with little, is for the reason mentioned.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:83: And the general teaching regarding intent is that a person should think, at the time of eating, that he eats before the King, and his eating is drawn from the table that is before the LORD; and thereby he will not become a glutton, for they compared in the Zohar the lower table to the supernal table — thus, just as from the supernal table the supernal souls and angels are nourished, so his soul is nourished from the supernal food that has been materialized in this lower table. This is (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:84: And there is a necessary support for this intent from the Zohar (portion Terumah, 156b) on the verse (Psalms 23:5), "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" — these are his words: a person's table earns him merit to eat at another table in the delight of that [World to Come], as it is said (2 Samuel 9:13), "for he ate continually at the king's table." And King David said, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" — the arrangement of the table [here] is in that world, for then is the delight and yearning by which the soul enjoys in the World to Come. And does a table exist for souls in that world? Yes, for the sustenance and provision of delight they eat in that world, just as the supernal angels eat; and do they eat of supernal bread? Yes; see there. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:85: And in this manner, in his eating he should intend that his eating comes from the Shechinah, from which sustenance is drawn down below to those lower, that every eating in this world [comes from her]. And though eating is found above — "eat, friends" (Song of Songs 5:1) — they have already answered this in portion Vayikra (Zohar 4a): one who has jugs of wine needs eating.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:86: Further, it is possible to explain the intent of eating by what they said, that the table is called an altar. They said in Berachot (54b): Rabbi Yehuda said, three things prolong a person's days and years: he who prolongs his prayer, he who lingers at his table, and he who lingers in the privy. And there he explained the proof for each one, and gave the reason for lingering at one's table: perhaps a poor man will come and he will give to him, as it is written (Ezekiel 41:22), "The altar was of wood, three cubits high," and it is written [further], "and he said to me, this is the table that is before the LORD" — it begins with "altar" and ends with "table." Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both said: as long as the Temple stood, the altar atoned for Israel; now, a person's table atones for him. Thus far his words. And so our Sages of blessed memory said: Rabbi Elazar said, when the Temple stood, the altar atoned for him; now that the Temple does not stand, one who merits it — his table atones for him, as it is said (Isaiah 58:7), "Is it not to share your bread with the hungry" — if he does not merit this, then "and bring the wandering poor into your house" [is fulfilled against him] — meaning, gentiles come and take by force. Thus far his words. Now, according to the plain meaning of the statement, if at the beginning of his eating he directs his intention that from that food he will give to a poor man, then his eating is a mitzvah, and the soul benefits from such a meal. On this basis we may offer a second interpretation of (Proverbs 13:25 [sic, 13:21]), "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — that when he eats, he intends to perform a mitzvah from that meal, so that his soul be satisfied from the mitzvah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:87: And they have already elaborated at length in the Zohar (portion Terumah, 155b) on the merit of one who feeds the poor at his table. They said, by what does a person merit to delight in that supernal delight? By his own table, by his delighting upon his table the souls of the poor, as it is written (Isaiah 58:10), "and satisfy the afflicted soul" — what is written after it? "Then you shall delight in the LORD." So too the Holy One, blessed be He, anoints him with all those delights of the oil of the great supernal holiness that flows and is continually drawn to that supernal glory. Thus far his words. This is "to the satisfaction of his soul" — just as he has satisfied an afflicted soul, so too his own soul will be satisfied from the supernal light.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:88: However, this works well when one can merit giving to a poor person; but if a person travels on a journey and has no poor person with him, or where poor people are not commonly found, such as at night when there are not so many poor people going about, or in a place where poor people are not present, what is his remedy so that his table be an altar? It is possible to say that he should estimate in his mind the value of the food that a poor man might have eaten, and give him money with which the poor man could buy the necessities of a meal. This is a valid device, and he should choose to give his bread or his money to a poor person who has some knowledge of Torah, and who knows how to recite Birkat HaMazon and the other blessings of enjoyment, and then the charity is acceptable, as we shall elaborate in its place.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:89: However, this device is a matter of intellectual reasoning, and the Gemara says only "perhaps a poor man will come and he will give to him" — the essential point being that he give from his own portion to a poor person, as it is written, "is it not to share your bread with the hungry" — from what you yourself eat. Furthermore, there is a difficulty: the poor man himself, who does not have enough even for himself alone — how can his own table atone for him?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:90: It is possible to resolve this by what they explained in the Zohar (portion Terumah, 153b), these are his words: a person's table must always be before him at the time he blesses the Holy One, blessed be He, so that blessing rest upon him from above, and it should not appear empty, for blessings from above do not rest in an empty place, as it is written (2 Kings 4:2), "tell me, what do you have in the house?" And the fellowship have established that regarding a table over which no words of Torah were said, it is written (Isaiah 28:8), "for all tables are full of filthy vomit, without a place" — and it is forbidden to bless over that table. Why? Because there is a table and there is a table: there is a table which one arranges before the Holy One, blessed be He, above, and it stands continually to arrange upon it the words of Torah and to include within it the letters of the words of Torah, and it gathers them within and includes them all within itself, and through them it is perfected and rejoices and has gladness. Of this table it is written (Ezekiel 41:22), "this is the table that is before the LORD" — before the LORD, and not merely "from before the LORD." There is another table which has no portion in Torah and has no portion in the holiness of Torah — this is "without a place," for it has no portion at all in the side of holiness. Therefore, a table over which no words of Torah are said is a table of filthy vomit, a table of idolatry; there is no portion for it in the secret of the Supernal God. But a table over which words of Torah were said, the Holy One, blessed be He, takes that table and makes it His portion, and moreover, the great appointed angel Suria takes those words and makes an image of that table before the Holy One, blessed be He, and all those words of Torah said over it rise upon that table and stand ready before the Holy One, blessed be He, the Holy King — this is the meaning of "this is the table that is before the LORD," that it stands ready before the Holy One, blessed be He. A person's table stands to purify the person from all his sins.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:91: Fortunate is he in whom these two stand upon his table: words of Torah, and a portion for the poor from that table. When that table is removed from before a person, two holy angels are stationed there, one on the right and one on the left. One says: this is the table of the Holy King, that so-and-so arranges before Him; may this table be arranged continually with supernal blessings and supernal oil and greatness — may the Holy One, blessed be He, rest upon it. And the other says: this is the table of the Holy King that so-and-so arranges before Him; this is the table which the supernal and lower beings shall bless it — may this table be arranged before the Ancient of Days in this world and in the World to Come. My father, when they would remove the table from before him, would cover it, and would say: raise up this table modestly, so it not be shamed before the messengers of the King. A person's table earns him the World to Come, earns him sustenance in this world, earns him recognition for good before the Ancient of Days, and earns him added strength and greatness where needed. Fortunate is the portion of that person in this world and in the World to Come. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:92: Behold, he said that a person's table stands to purify him from all his sins — and this certainly refers to occupying oneself with Torah at the table before Birkat HaMazon, for they said that a table over which no words of Torah were said, it is forbidden to bless over that table — it appears this certainly refers to before Birkat HaMazon. And from here also there is a demolition of one who wrote that through Birkat HaMazon one fulfills the obligation of saying words of Torah at a table where none were said, as is clear. And up to now he has not spoken of the portion for the poor, but only afterward said, "fortunate is he in whom these two stand upon his table" — and we have already explained above the nature of the word "fortunate" [zakhai], meaning "more praiseworthy." We find, then, that wherever there are no poor people, or he himself is poor, his table becomes an altar to atone for his sins by his occupying himself with Torah there, and it is fitting that it be called an altar — for just as the altar is called an altar because sacrifices are slaughtered upon it, so through occupying himself with Torah a person slaughters his evil inclination, as he said (Sukkah 52b): if this loathsome one accosts you, drag him to the study hall — if he is [as hard as] a stone, he will melt. And Torah also atones for sins more than all sacrifices, as it is said (1 Samuel 3:14), "the iniquity of the house of Eli shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering" — and they explained (Rosh Hashanah 18a): but it is atoned for through words of Torah, for words of Torah are superior to all sacrifices, as explained in portion Kedoshim (80b); see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:93: And in Midrash Ruth (5:15), they said (Ruth 3:7), "And Boaz ate and drank, and his heart was glad" — why was his heart glad? Because he blessed over his food. Another interpretation: his heart was glad because he ate sweet things after the meal, which loosen the tongue for Torah. Another interpretation: his heart was glad because he occupied himself with words of Torah, as it is said (Psalms 119:72), "the Torah of Your mouth is good to me." Thus far his words. And it is possible that all these are so.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:94: Also, if he is a penitent, he should confess before eating — this too slaughters his evil inclination. And so Rabbeinu Yonah wrote in Sefer HaYirah, that a penitent must confess beforehand and search through what he has done up to that time. Through this he will not become a glutton, since he will think of his sins, which are many, and that he is not worthy on account of his sins of that food, but only because of the great kindness of Him who feeds both the wicked and the good. This is the matter of (Pesachim 118a), "a person's sustenance is as difficult as the splitting of the Red Sea," as explained in the Zohar (portion Terumah, 170a) — that it is difficult before the Holy One, blessed be He, that is, the Shechinah, who judges the world to sustain it because of the wickedness of its deeds. Through this he slaughters his evil inclination, and the table becomes for him an altar of atonement.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:95: Also, Rabbeinu Yonah wrote (ibid.) that while he still craves to eat, he should relinquish some of his desire for the honor of the Creator. This too slaughters his evil inclination and atones for him, for he certainly slaughters his physical desire, and it is written (Psalms 50:23), "He who sacrifices thanksgiving honors Me" — and they explained (Sanhedrin 43b): whoever slaughters his evil inclination and confesses honors the Holy One, blessed be He, in both worlds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:96: From the statement of the Zohar that we have copied, you will see the greatness of the early sages, peace be upon them, that they weighed matters according to their spirituality, not according to their physicality — for they said that they would cover the table so it be done modestly, this being because of the spiritual holiness upon it, since it had become a base for holiness in that words of Torah were said over it and a portion of it given to the poor. And the spirituality of the mitzvah performed at that table is that the angels ascend, and the two angels — one corresponding to the Torah and the other to the portion of the poor — the one corresponding to the portion of the poor blesses him with worldly blessings, measure for measure, and this is what is meant by "may this table be arranged continually with supernal blessings." And corresponding to the Torah he said, "this is the table of the Holy King" — this being the holy Torah that flowed from it and rises higher and higher; therefore he said, "may this table be arranged before the Ancient of Days."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:97: And what he said at the end of the statement, "and earns him added strength and greatness where needed" — this refers to the Shechinah, who requires the arousal of the lower beings, and before her sustenance is difficult, as explained. Therefore, since these [Torah and charity] are dedicated to her, they add strength to her from above, for these two are essentially rooted in the Tree of Life and are all from the right side.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:98: The Torah — as explained by the Faithful Shepherd (portion Pinchas, end of 245), who said that the table is judgment [din] in the north, and one must bind Torah, which is from the right, to it. These are his words: but in the secrets of Torah they established, one who wishes to become wealthy should face north, and place his table in the north — thus the table is to the left, which is judgment, and one must bind to it the right, which is Torah, given from Chesed, which is mercy, "the right hand of the LORD." Thus far his words. And in the Zohar (portion Ekev, 273) they explained regarding this matter, that Torah is YHVH from the right; the table is Adonai from the left — thus the intent is the union of the two Names YAHDONHAI: "then you shall call and the LORD shall answer" (Isaiah 58:9).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:99: And likewise, charity is the Tree of Life, as explained in portion Bechukotai (113b) and several other places, and we shall copy his words in its place. And there (Zohar, portion Beshalach, 62a), that charity, which is loving-kindness [gemilut chasadim], is from the side of Chesed — they said, the sustenance that is higher than it, that is finer still, and comes from the place where judgment rests, and is called "tzedek" — this is the sustenance of the poor. And the secret of the matter: whoever completes the poor man [gives him what he lacks] completes for him the letter vav, and it is made into tzedakah. And this secret is "he who is kind rewards his own soul" [gomel nafsho ish chesed] — meaning loving-kindness — for it rests in judgment, and he completes it with kindness; then it becomes mercy. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:100: Thus we find that through these two commandments a person gives strength above, and by this we may offer a third interpretation of "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — to give satisfaction to his supernal soul through Torah and charity, in the manner they explained in the Zohar (ibid., portion Terumah, 128b) that "the rock of my heart and my portion" (Psalms 73:26), and "a good heart" (Proverbs 15:15), and "and his heart was glad" (Ruth 3:7) — all these refer to the Holy One, blessed be He; likewise we may say that "his soul" refers to the Holy One, blessed be He — this being to add strength and greatness where needed, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:101: Further I have heard another way, that all his meals be for the sake of a mitzvah, by doing as Shammai the Elder did, of whom they said that all his days he ate in honor of Shabbat. How so? If he found a fine animal he would say, this is for the honor of Shabbat; if he found another finer than it, etc. (Beitzah 16a). We find in this device that his meal is a mitzvah, for sometimes he would need to restrain his desires for the honor of Shabbat, such as when he did not find another finer than it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:102: One must understand what is praiseworthy in this, for at first glance it would have been better for him to leave both the first and the second for Shabbat — what benefit is there in his eating the first one that was designated for the honor of Shabbat? And even if a finer one had not become available to him, then he would not have eaten in honor of Shabbat at all, and it would have been fitting to say that all his days he set aside for Shabbat.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:103: But in truth this is no difficulty, for certainly if the second animal would not have sufficed him for Shabbat, he certainly would have left both; rather, certainly the second one would suffice him, and therefore he ate the first.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:104: The reason for the possibility of this matter is found in what they said in the Mechilta (portion Yitro), regarding (Exodus 20:8), "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy" — you shall remember it from the first day of the week, that if a fine portion becomes available to you, you should set it aside for Shabbat — and we have copied the rest of his words above in chapter 2. And this was the opinion of Shammai the Elder. And so they said there in the Gemara: it was also taught thus, Beit Shammai say, from the first day of your week [set aside] for your Shabbat, and Beit Hillel say (Psalms 68:20), "Blessed be the LORD, day by day He bears our burden." And Rashi, peace be upon him, explained: "from the first day of your week for your Shabbat" — from the first day of your week, set your heart toward the coming Shabbat. And we have already explained there (ch. 2) the reason for the possibility of remembering Shabbat every day, and that reason suffices for the possibility of this designation. But regarding the eating, we may say, as explained there, that a person's eating on Shabbat is not equal to his eating on a weekday, for Shabbat eating is called "oneg" [delight], and it is the secret of "Eden, river, garden" [the initial letters of oneg], as it is said (Isaiah 58:13), "and you shall call the Sabbath a delight," and it is a mitzvah. Now, when he designates on the first day of the week a portion for Shabbat, the holiness of Shabbat rests upon it; and when he finds another one finer than it for Shabbat and eats the first, he purifies his eating with the holiness of Shabbat eating, which is spiritual eating and a mitzvah. And one of the things that save the bodies of the righteous from worms ruling over them in their death is that they enjoy only meals that are mitzvot, and meals of Shabbat and festivals, and at the very least he enjoys this benefit — that people cannot say "take what you chose for yourself," since he enjoyed only a meal of mitzvah, which is Shabbat.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:105: And if you say, but if a fine portion does not become available to him, then he will not eat in honor of Shabbat at all — one may answer that the Holy One, blessed be He, joins a good thought to the deed (Kiddushin 40a), and for this reason it was brought, "it was also taught thus, from the first day of your week for your Shabbat," and Rashi, of blessed memory, explained, "set your heart toward the coming Shabbat" — he did not say that one should by all means seek to designate something for Shabbat, but rather that he should set his heart that the first portion that becomes available to him will be for Shabbat.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:106: And this matter is exactly what they explained in the Mechilta on "Remember" — that the remembrance is in the heart, that he not forget from his heart the matter of Shabbat, because of its allusion to the world that is entirely long [i.e., eternal], toward the world that is entirely Shabbat. And even when only one portion becomes available to him, by his designating it for Shabbat he eats it for the sake of Shabbat, for since it was possible for him to eat it and not leave it for the honor of Shabbat, we find that he eats it for the sake of the holiness of Shabbat. And likewise, when he designates the second for Shabbat and does not eat it, we find that he eats the first for the honor of Shabbat, since he left the second. Thus we find in this that the end of the deed reflects the beginning of the thought, for in the supernal thought Shabbat preceded, and afterward the six days of labor; but at the end of the deed, then the beginning of the thought is revealed. Therefore, every single day, Shabbat comes first in his thought, and he sets his heart to eat in honor of Shabbat, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:107: Also, when a person gives from his meal to a poor person, his meal becomes a mitzvah, and so did Rabbi Tanchum, as explained in the Midrash, Vayikra Rabbah (portion Behar 34:5), on the verse "and if your brother becomes poor" (Leviticus 25:35). These are his words: this is what Rabbi Tanchum ben Rabbi Chiya used to do — when his mother would buy him a pound of meat from the market, she would buy two, one for the poor and one for him, because of "God has made the one alongside the other" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) — the poor and the rich, so that they might earn merit through one another. Therefore Moses warns Israel, "and if your brother becomes poor." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:108: Now, through this a person will be saved from having his belly turned upon his face in his grave after three days, as they said in the Zohar (portion Vayakhel, 199b), these are his words: after three days, that filth turns upon his face and says to him, "take back what you gave me — you ate and drank every day and gave nothing to the poor, and all your days were like festivals and holidays, while the poor were as though hungry, not eating with you — take back what you gave me." This is what is written (Malachi 2:3), "and I will spread dung upon your faces, the dung of your festivals" — and this has already been established. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:109: And in the Zohar (portion Vayakhel, 218a) it is explained that on the six weekdays the Shechinah benefits from Birkat HaMazon, but on Shabbat the Shechinah benefits from the very meal in which a person delights, so that whatever a person delights in on Shabbat performs a mitzvah. On this basis we may also read "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" [as meaning] that his soul, which is the Shechinah, is satisfied from Birkat HaMazon. These are his words: Rabbi Yosi opened and said (Ruth 3:7), "And Boaz ate and drank and his heart was glad" — what is "and his heart was glad"? That he blessed over his food, as they established, and this is the secret that whoever blesses over his food thereby gladdens his heart. And who is this? As it is written (Psalms 27:8), "to You my heart says," and it is written (ibid. 73:26), "the rock of my heart and my portion" — for the blessing over food is beloved before the Holy One, blessed be He; whoever blesses after being satisfied gladdens and rejoices another place, and your sign is: the meal of Shabbat in another place benefits from that blessing of satisfaction. Why? Because sustenance is difficult before the Holy One, blessed be He, in that place; and once a person eats and drinks and recites that blessing, it rises and benefits from those words of satisfaction, and thus he benefits from sustenance both from below and from above. This is the secret known to the fellowship — the secret that on a weekday one benefits only from those words that ascend from being satisfied, and they are all crowned and filled and satisfied with joy, and that place benefits from them. On Shabbat it is a different secret — in the actual food itself, and in that joy of the food of the mitzvah of Shabbat, as they established.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:110: Whoever blesses the Holy One, blessed be He, after being satisfied must direct his heart and place his will in joy, and should not be found sad, but should bless in joy through this secret, and should set his will [knowing] that he is now giving to another in joy and with a good eye — just as he blesses in joy and with a good eye, so is he given in joy and with a good eye; and therefore he should not be found sad at all, but in joy and with words of Torah, and he should set his heart and his will to give this blessing through the needed secret.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:111: The secret here: the four chariots that rule in the four directions are nourished from that blessing of satisfaction, and through those words of "Blessed are You" they benefit and grow and are crowned by it. And whoever blesses must have will in joy and with a good eye, and therefore (Proverbs 22:9), "he who has a good eye shall be blessed" — and here [read] the end of the verse [connected to its beginning]: "for he gives of his bread to the poor" — for if you do not say so, this verse's beginning and end would not connect. Rather, "he who has a good eye" — as we have established — "shall be blessed," certainly with a good eye and in joy, and he does not bless in joy for nothing, for from that blessing and that joy "he gives of his bread to the poor" — a place to be nourished from all sides, a place that has nothing of its own, a place that benefits from all sides and is included from all sides. These matters are entrusted only to the wise, to know the way of Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:112: Come and see: Boaz had a good eye, and there was no hardness of forehead in him at all. What is written? (Ruth 3:7) "And he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain" — the secret of which is written (Song of Songs 7:3), "your belly is a heap of wheat." From here we learn that whoever blesses Birkat HaMazon properly, in joy, with the will of the heart, when he departs this world, a place is prepared for him among the supernal secrets in the holy chambers. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:113: And when you understand what is said, "thus he benefits from sustenance both from below and from above," which is explained in portion Noach (60a-b) on the verse (Proverbs 5:15), "drink waters from your own cistern," you will understand the sweetness of the honeycomb of "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul." We have taken care to copy the whole statement, since it explains the intent of Birkat HaMazon in what is said, "the secret here: the four chariots that rule in the four directions are nourished from that blessing of satisfaction," etc., and therefore his reward in the World to Come is what is said at the end of the statement, "a place is prepared for him among the supernal secrets in the holy chambers." Also, what is said, that he should bless with a good eye, is understood by what is said in the Idra (portion Naso, 130a), that "a good eye" refers to Arich [Anpin]; see there. For this, a good eye, will, and joy are needed, in order to draw down from the first three [supernal attributes].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:114: Now, if a person intends at the beginning of the eating that he eats in order to bless the place that needs blessing, so that it be drawn from above — this is like the parable of the wet-nurse: when she has someone to nurse, the milk in her breasts increases — this too is a correct intent, and it is along the lines of what is explained in the Zohar (portion Beshalach, 62a), that a person is obligated to ask for his sustenance every day, since by his asking he causes sustenance to be drawn from above so that it may be given to him. And it is already known that sustenance is dependent on fate [mazal], as they said (Mo'ed Katan 28a), "children, life, and sustenance... depend on fate," etc. He said, these are his words: Rabbi Yosi opened (Psalms 145:16), "You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing with favor" — what is written above it? "The eyes of all look to You expectantly" — all those beings of the world wait and lift their eyes to the Holy One, blessed be He. Therefore all these people of faith need, every single day, to ask for their sustenance from the Holy One, blessed be He, and to pray their prayer over it. Why? Because whoever prays his prayer to the Holy One, blessed be He, for his sustenance causes that Tree from which sustenance for all comes to be blessed every day, and the reason for the matter is "Blessed be the LORD, day by day" (Psalms 68:20) — even though it [the blessing] is already found with him [the Tree], he must still ask before the Holy One, blessed be He, and pray for sustenance every day, so that blessings be found with it [renewed] every single day above. And therefore a person should not cook sustenance from one day to another, nor delay from one day to another — this is what is written (Exodus 16:4), "and the people went out and gathered a portion for each day," except from Shabbat eve for Shabbat, as we have established — and then the Holy One, blessed be He, is found full of blessings every day, and then it is written, "You open Your hand," etc. What is "favor" [ratzon]? That favor found from the Ancient Holy One, from which favor issues to provide sustenance for all. And whoever asks for sustenance every single day is called a faithful son — a son for whose sake blessings are found above. Thus far his words.
